title: Trump Weighs 'Massive' Iran Escalation as War Enters Critical Phase
excerpt: The US president says he is close to ordering the largest strike yet against Iran, even as back-channel talks gain traction through Pakistan and China.
body:
• US missiles struck Iran for a 13th consecutive night on Friday as Trump told reporters he was "locked and loaded" but had not yet decided on a major escalation.
  • Houthi attacks on Saudi tankers in the Red Sea drove oil above $100 a barrel, opening a dangerous new front in the conflict.
  • CIA and DIA assessments conclude the current bombing campaign is unlikely to shift Iran's negotiating posture, leaving the White House with few good options.
  • Pakistan is exploring a diplomatic path to restart stalled US-Iran talks following a push initiated by China.

US missiles struck targets across Iran on Friday for a 13th straight night, killing at least four people in the city of Ahvaz, as President Donald Trump signalled he was nearing a decision on whether to dramatically escalate the five-month-old war.

"I am considering a massive attack. Bigger than anything we have ever had before. I am close to making a decision," Trump told Israel's Channel 12 on Thursday. Hours later, speaking to reporters at the White House, he offered a more tempered assessment: "We are talking to them. I think they're being serious."

But he added: "We're locked and loaded. We're ready to go."

Escalation Spiral Deepens

The strikes on Friday hit a Revolutionary Guards Navy headquarters in the Caspian Sea province of Gilan and the port city of Bandar Anzali, according to Iranian media. Iran responded by firing at US bases across the region — targeting Camp Buehring and Camp Arifjan in Kuwait, a US barracks in Jordan, and a surveillance tower used by the US Fifth Fleet in Bahrain.

https://x.com/kilmeade/status/2080672830299963853

Jordan's army said it intercepted seven Iranian missiles and six drones, reporting no casualties. Kuwait said its air defences were intercepting "hostile" targets launched from Iran.

The war has now killed 18 US service members and wounded more than 500, according to officials who spoke to Reuters. Iran's health ministry said 59 people had been killed and 666 wounded since fighting resumed in late June after the collapse of an interim truce.

"There's a military exit where we just keep going just the way we are, and we can even make it a heavier dose. Or there's a smarter strategy — that you make a deal."

— Donald Trump, speaking at the White House on Friday

Oil Markets Rattled by Houthi Blockade

The conflict widened sharply this week when Houthi forces in Yemen announced a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia and claimed strikes on two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea's Bab el-Mandeb Strait on Thursday. The attacks drove Brent crude above $100 a barrel for the first time since May, though prices eased to around $96 by Friday afternoon. US retail gasoline has climbed past $4 a gallon.

The Bab el-Mandeb Strait had served as a critical relief valve, allowing Saudi Arabia to reroute oil by pipeline to the Red Sea while Iran maintained its near-total blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. Tanker traffic through Hormuz fell to just one vessel on Thursday — the lowest since May 7.

Shipping insurance costs through the southern Red Sea doubled for some companies, and several tankers reversed course to take the far longer route around Africa via the Suez Canal.

Intelligence Agencies Doubt Bombing's Effectiveness

The White House faces an uncomfortable reality. Both the CIA and the Defense Intelligence Agency have recently assessed that the current bombing campaign is unlikely to shift Tehran's negotiating position, according to two US officials familiar with the assessments, as reported by CNN.

Meanwhile, Qatar — the key mediator between Washington and Tehran — has threatened to walk away from talks after Iran struck a Qatari tanker earlier this month. The potential loss of Doha's mediation could be "devastating and possibly irreplaceable" for diplomatic efforts, officials said.

"This is a bombing campaign in search of a strategy. More bombing will not convince Iran to open the Strait of Hormuz or to give us the deal we want — it will only harden their position."

— Joe Kent, former Trump administration appointee

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking in Manila after an ASEAN foreign ministers meeting, struck a harder line. "The president's policy is a head for an eye," Rubio told reporters, updating the biblical formula of reciprocal justice. "They will pay a very heavy price."

Pakistan Steps Into Diplomatic Vacuum

As the Qatari channel frays, Pakistan has emerged as a potential new mediator. Reuters reported that Islamabad is exploring a path towards resuming stalled talks between Washington and Tehran, following a push initiated by China. Exploratory discussions took place during a visit by Iran's Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni to Islamabad this week — his second within 10 days.

The diplomatic manoeuvring underscores the widening regional dimensions of a war that began on February 28 as a joint US-Israeli operation but has since drawn in Gulf states, Yemen's Houthis, and now South Asian powers.

Economic Toll Mounts

The financial burden is accelerating. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth told the Senate Appropriations Committee on Tuesday that the war's cost has reached $37.5 billion, up from an estimated $30 billion in June. The White House has asked Congress for $87 billion in supplemental funding under tight deadlines.

Moody's Analytics estimates the total cost to American consumers and taxpayers — including rising prices, interest-rate hikes, and military spending — has reached at least $132 billion.

"The cost of this war has been astronomical, and what has it been for?" asked Senator Patty Murray of Washington, the committee's vice chair. "President Trump has, by any objective measure, failed to achieve his goals."

Treasury yields climbed to 18-month highs this week as the conflict stoked inflation fears. Analysts at investment firm Yardeni Research framed the moment as a choice between "Apocalypse Now" and "TACO" — "Trump always chickens out" — a pattern markets have come to expect from the president on tariffs and military brinkmanship alike.

What Comes Next

Trump has threatened to expand targets to include Iranian energy plants, bridges, and the deep-underground nuclear-linked site known as Pickaxe Mountain near Natanz. He has also floated sending ground forces to seize Kharg Island, through which roughly 90% of Iran's oil exports flow.

Analysts note that Iran is fighting an asymmetric war — escalating horizontally by striking US allies and Gulf infrastructure even as its own air defences are degraded. That strategy is designed to rally international pressure against Washington rather than match American firepower directly.

For the Indian diaspora, the stakes extend well beyond geopolitics. India imports roughly 85% of its crude oil, and every sustained spike in global prices feeds directly into domestic inflation and fuel costs. The disruption of both the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb corridor threatens supply chains that millions of Indian workers in the Gulf depend on for their livelihoods.

With Pakistan now entering the diplomatic picture and China pushing behind the scenes, the conflict's resolution — or further escalation — will ripple across South Asia and the broader Indian Ocean region in the weeks ahead.
nri_angle: Sustained oil price spikes from the Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb disruptions threaten India's energy costs and the livelihoods of millions of Indian workers in the Gulf, while Pakistan's emergence as a mediator adds a South Asian dimension to the conflict.
author: Diaspora Desk
